comments.body: @orlitzky I have read your proposal in https://github.com/sagemath/sage/discussions/41067 to create separately buildable Sage add-on packages, an example of which is your sagemath-giac, with interest. Happy to inform you that this is already implemented – [for all libraries and dependencies of Sage](https://github.com/passagemath#passagemath-in-the-mathematical-software-landscape) – successfully in passagemath, and all that without the intrusiveness of moving everything to individual repositories.

Yes but having them so closely integrated with the distribution eliminates many of the benefits that I perceive, as I'm sure you remember.

Having separate, independent packages like sagemath-giac should make life easier for you, no? It's one less thing for you to maintain as a fork. There are several others that would be "easy" to split off in the same manner. It's trivial to copy/paste, say, `sage.libs.coxeter3` into a new repo -- most of the work on sagemath-giac was replacing old cruft, trying to write nice docs, and updating the tests to run in a plain python shell.

Anything independent enough to be split like that could be shared.

> Having separate, independent packages like sagemath-giac should make life easier for you, no? It's one less thing for you to maintain as a fork.

I would still need to fork it because, as you are surely aware, your product is not viable as a Python package. It does not publish wheels on PyPI and moreover depends on the monolithic Sage package, which publishes no wheels on PyPI:

- at build time, declared https://github.com/sagemath/sagemath-giac/blob/main/pyproject.toml#L7 build time dependency on **sagemath-standard**
  - which, by the way, was just killed as part of #1508 

- at runtime, undeclared.

> There are several others that would be "easy" to split off in the same manner. It's trivial to copy/paste, say, `sage.libs.coxeter3` into a new repo

Yes, it's all easy for the one developer who decides to split it off. But, as I am sure I explained many times in the past, it creates additional friction for anyone else among the Sage developers because they now have to navigate another repo; and no one asked for that.

By the way, have you even notified the original author about **sagemath-giac**?

Edit: Also, in your README you are linking to the wrong project where you write "For many years, SageMath has included an interface to Giac based on the GiacPy python interface by Frederic Han: https://pypi.org/project/giacpy/ "

Edit: Your project's metadata is also missing information about authors and maintainers, and there is no indication about CONTRIBUTING, creating ambiguity about what procedures apply. Is it a single-maintainer package where you call the shots? Do the review procedures of the Sage project apply? (Many of the other separate packages in github.com/sagemath had the same issues, until I fixed them by adding files like this: https://github.com/sagemath/cypari2/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

> having them so closely integrated with the distribution eliminates many of the benefits that I perceive, as I'm sure you remember.

Yes, I do remember this rhetorical spin about the bootstrapping phase, and the related grandstanding that blocked at least one of my PRs, no worries.

If Mr. "no version synchronization is the best version synchronization" wants to be helpful, he could oppose the gratuitous incompatibility of basic packages such as `cysignals` with older Python versions - https://github.com/sagemath/cysignals/pull/233

I just come across this. While I'm mildly inconvenienced (that I'm still on Python 3.11), spec 0 is endorsed by many of sage's dependencies (at least ipython).

What reason do you have against it? Since currently sage doesn't formally endorse spec 0 (nor does it seem), I suppose we could have a discussion on whether to formally adopt this, or be more conservative.

(Note that spec 0 promote "convenience for developers", and since it's ultimately developers who will decide whether to accept your decision, you should try to list reasons that appeal to developers.)

SPEC 0 is for packages in the scientific Python community that wish to synchronize around a faster drop schedule so that access to newer language/library features becomes possible.
None of this applies to cysignals. It is a package without dependencies and without any relation to the scientific Python ecosystem. And it is the only package in the sagemath organization that has found relatively widespread adoption in random Cython projects because it provides a missing feature in a reusable way. Regardless of drop schedule decisions for Sage itself, it should therefore be tied to the version support schedule of Cython itself.

comments.body:
Yes, the limit for wheels on PyPI is just 100 MB.

More importantly, multi-GB wheels, even if PyPI allowed them, would be a very poor fit for the PyPI "ecosystem", where virtual environments tend to be created frequently and separate virtual environments are used for separate projects.

For a project, depending on any functionality of the Sage library comes with a large cost (undeployability), so it is generally avoided when there are lighter-weight alternatives. 

Projects that do use the Sage library typically only use a small fraction of the functionality, as is witnessed by the existing published projects that depend on the Sage library (https://github.com/passagemath/passagemath/issues/248). 


I've written more about this in my ICMS 2024 paper "The Reformation of Sage", https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-64529-7_1

The build for the HiGHS python bindings is separate from the C++ code. For python, you should specify  
```
-DPYTHON_BUILD_SETUP=ON 
```
in the CMake flags. It is a separate library for the moment, so you may have to include both if you are using HiGHS both from python and C. Not all features in the C/C++ are available in Python already, like HiPO.

Thanks for taking a look. This failure is, however, unrelated to highspy. Apologies for not providing enough context.

I am building HiGHS for mingw32 and then link it into a Cython module using the native Windows toolchain (MSVC). This second step is failing with the indicated error.
I'll note that the same build for the Windows ARM64 architecture succeeds.

On ARM64, is the same toolchain used, for the successful case? If MSVC is used for the cython module, then MSVC should be used for highs lib as well. A mismatch between MinGW and MSVC would suggest the error is expected

Hello!

Thanks for reaching out, and for the proposal!

 I've mirror the request in CodeBerg https://codeberg.org/guix/guix/issues/6276

We are working on migration for Python 3.11 -> 3.12 which is hard requirement for a fresh version of SageMath.

I'll take a look at `passagemath` (license, missing dependencies etc) we may keep them together.
Note passagemath supports Python 3.11–3.14

> Each of the ~120 modularized distribution packages is provided on PyPI ...

PyPI is not hard requirement the recent change to Python build system allows us to prepare Guix package directly from source distributed by VCS.

Some initial question after a quick glance:

Is `passagemath-standard` (https://pypi.org/project/passagemath-standard/#files) a PyPI repository for https://github.com/passagemath/passagemath, I guess?

Is it a WIP fork or you try to upstream changes as much as you can by keeping some of the metadata still pointing to SageMath
https://github.com/passagemath/passagemath/blob/b7105d1b4cd8de9d3ec76e83d7303a11612b4427/pyproject.toml#L83-L88

The top-level pyproject.toml is inherited from the upstream project and not directly used in the passagemath build.

https://github.com/passagemath/passagemath/tree/main/pkgs
